title: Star, moon, sun
hook: the young Ibrahim watches a star, the moon, the sun set, and says he will not love what sets (6:76–79)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kan'an, the son on the mountain, and the wave that came between him and his father. Today, a new prophet, and a night sky.

Lie on your back somewhere dark, far from the city. The first star comes out, so bright you'd swear it was a plane. Later the moon rises, huge and orange, and the star looks small. In the morning the sun swallows them both. By evening, the sun is gone too. Long ago, a young man watched that same sky and asked a question. His name was Ibrahim, Abraham, a prophet honored by Jews, Christians and Muslims alike.
screen: `THE FIRST STAR, SO BRIGHT.` → `THE MOON, THEN THE SUN.` → `A YOUNG MAN LOOKING UP.`

segments.voice: Surah six. Ibrahim lives among people who worship idols and the lights of the sky. Night falls, and he sees a star. This is my Lord, he says. Then the star sets, and he says, in Pickthall's words: “I love not things that set.” The moon rises, brighter: this is my Lord. The moon sets. Then the sun, blazing: this is my Lord, this one is greater. And the sun goes down too. So he turns away from all of it, toward the One who made the heavens and the earth, as one by nature upright. The Arabic word is hanif: the one who leans toward God, and away from everything else. Scholars read this scene two ways, and both are old. Some say it's a young man truly searching, trying each light in turn, until he sees that anything that disappears can't be God. Others point to the verses around it. His people worshipped the stars, and Ibrahim, they say, already knew. He was walking them through their own logic out loud, star by star, so they could hear where it led. Either way, his test is simple enough for a child. Does it set? Does it fade, or leave, or go dark? Then it can't be the thing you give your whole heart to. His word for things that set, afilin, also means things that fade and vanish. It's a question you can ask of almost anything you love too much.
screen: `A STAR, AND IT SETS.` · `THE MOON, THE SUN: GONE TOO.` · `SEARCHING, OR TEACHING?` · `HANIF — LEANING TOWARD GOD.` · then, large: `I LOVE NOT THINGS THAT SET.`

segments.voice: If you can, look out a window at the sky, day or night; if not, picture the last sky you saw. Watch the light for a few slow breaths, and notice that even up there, things are moving. If you pray, turn your face, as Ibrahim did, toward the One who made it all.
Star. The first light Ibrahim saw set, then the moon, then the sun, and he said: I love not things that set.
Your line: love what doesn't set. Ibrahim's whole test fits in three words: does it set? See you tomorrow.

original.note: Arabic: "I love not things that set" (6:76); afilin are things that sink, fade and vanish.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient man who worshipped the stars before he knew better.
what it means: star — the first of three lights Ibrahim watched set, until he said: I love not things that set.
what a scholar hears: an old debate, searcher or teacher, turning on 6:74–83, which calls it an argument given to Ibrahim against his people; afilin, things that fade; and hanif, the upright one.

notes: Pickthall 6:76 quoted from memory ('When the night grew dark upon him he beheld a star. He said: This is my Lord. But when it set, he said: I love not things that set.'). Confirm.

Two readings (a searcher reasoning his way; or a debater using his people's premises, supported by 6:83): both are classical (e.g. al-Tabari and al-Razi discuss them). Many scholars hold prophets never associated partners with God, favoring the second. Confirm the balance.
'The prophet the Qur'an names more than almost any other': Musa is named most; Ibrahim is among the most named (about 69 times). Confirm phrasing.
'The one Jews, Christians and Muslims all call their father in faith': a shared-neighbor note, no comparison. Confirm.
howItsDone: Ibrahim is named in the salat al-ibrahimiyya at the end of the prayer (Sunni practice; Shia tashahhud differs). Confirm the wording 'in every prayer'.
